findings.summary: Every author from Managing Partner to Office Manager writes in one literary register, built on the balanced antithesis and the aphoristic closing turn, so the corpus reads as one stylist wearing thirteen names.
findings.evidence: Hill: 'adjust the account with you, never around you' (d:0002). Macias: 'so the language sits on how they actually speak rather than on our guess at it' (d:0068). Le: 'a warm approach draws more candor than a cold one' (d:0085). Zimmerman: 'I would rather carry whichever you consider final than a number a reporter could check against the record' (d:0052). Even the office manager's badge-access note: 'I will take it up with the management office directly instead of leaving you waiting at the door' (d:0030).

findings.summary: Five kickoff memos by five different authors across seven years reuse the same signature first-person asides; these are personal framing sentences, not form fields, so it reads as one generator rather than a memo template.
findings.evidence: 'so nobody waits on a hand-off that was never assigned' (d:0003 Valenzuela 2017; verbatim d:0046 Bradley 2022; 'never made' variants d:0063 Macias, d:0076 Rose). 'None of that is new to us, but it is worth stating once at the start' (d:0003; near-verbatim d:0046, d:0063, d:0076). 'we log what we send so the record stays in order as the volume grows' (d:0003 and d:0046, verbatim). All five open the how-we-run section 'A word (first) on how we...' (d:0003, d:0039, d:0046, d:0063, d:0076).

findings.summary: All six engagements' opening client emails, by six different authors from 2017 to 2024, run the same script: open the thread to keep updates in one place, log the contacts for the file, report 'we have made a start', promise a steady cadence, ask one question, offer a short call.
findings.evidence: 'each note will be tied to the piece of work it concerns, so the thread stays easy to follow' appears verbatim in d:0004 (Valenzuela, 2017) and d:0064 (Macias, 2023). 'A short call works if that is easier than writing it out' closes d:0004, d:0040 (Carter), and d:0064, three authors. All six open with 'I am opening/starting this thread' or 'I wanted to open a thread' ... 'in one place'.

findings.summary: First-person status-report narration recurs verbatim across different authors writing to different clients, past what a house report skeleton would explain; the metric flagged only d:0015/d:0024, but the pattern spans four authors.
findings.evidence: 'The one thing I need from you next is your team's comments on the core narrative draft. With those in hand(,) the second half moves quickly' closes both d:0015 (Valenzuela, for Barrera) and d:0024 (Morris, for Castaneda) word for word. 'Three things are worth naming now, while each is still easy to manage/small... each has a plan sitting against it' opens the risk section in d:0015, d:0042 (Carter), and d:0056 (Bradley). The risk label 'A live announcement in the window' recurs in d:0015, d:0022, d:0024 across two engagements.

findings.summary: Every author works the client approver's full name into the email body with the same notarial 'For the file / For the record' device, addressing the correspondent by their own full name mid-message; the fact placement is mandated, but the identical workaround across eight authors is the voice leak.
findings.evidence: 'For the file, final approval on the messaging sits with you, Mary Frank' (d:0005, Rose). 'For the record, I will treat approvals as yours to give, Sandra Mcdaniel' (d:0047, Bradley). 'For the record I have Sandra Mcdaniel as the sign-off on the financial lines' (d:0052, Zimmerman). 'For the file, sign-off on the Suarez-Jones messaging stays with you, Jennifer Herrera' (d:0068, Macias), each written to that same person.

findings.summary: Distinctive personal asides recur nearly verbatim across different authors in unrelated genres years apart, which the same-genre similarity metric is structurally blind to.
findings.evidence: 'It is unglamorous work, and we are rather proud of how well we do it' (d:0007, Hill, 2017 firm overview) against 'It is unglamorous work, and it is the reason a job this heavy on email has stayed legible' (d:0073, Macias, 2023 status report). 'read like the company speaking and not like an agency writing on its behalf' (d:0015, Valenzuela status report) against 'reads as the company speaking and not as an agency writing on its behalf' (d:0022, Morris briefing deck).

findings.summary: The high-overlap pairs the metric flagged within Julie Hill's own genres read as legitimate self-template reuse, and the surface voice layer does differentiate: greetings, closings, and list habits track the style specs, and meeting minutes are the one genre with genuinely distinct voices.
findings.evidence: Engagement letters d:0002/d:0045/d:0061/d:0075 and onboarding records d:0034/d:0036/d:0060 are all authored by Hill, boilerplate genres a real principal would recycle. Macias opens 'Good morning Jennifer,' (d:0064), Zimmerman writes listless long paragraphs (d:0048), Morris numbers his lists (d:0024). Black's conversational minutes ('We were glad of that.', d:0027) against Suarez's procedural ones ('Nancy Suarez chaired and kept these minutes.', d:0041) are the corpus at its most multi-voiced.
